result.markdown: --- format: live-html: webr: packages: - survival --- # Missing data {#sec-missing} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: ::: {.callout-tip icon="false"} ## You need this chapter if… - `coxph()` reports that **observations were deleted due to missingness**, and it's more than a handful; - a **confounder** you need for matching or adjustment has missing values; - you're wondering whether to just analyse the complete cases. *This chapter builds on Chapter 3, and on Chapters 5–7 for the section on matching.* ::: ::: {.callout-note icon="false"} ## In this chapter **The question.** Real datasets have gaps. What does R do with them by default, when does that give the wrong answer, and what should you do instead? **By the end of this chapter you will be able to:** - spot how many patients a model has silently dropped; - explain the three kinds of missing data (MCAR, MAR, MNAR), and when a complete-case analysis is biased; - carry out **multiple imputation** with the **mice** package, including the survival outcome correctly, and pool the results; - combine multiple imputation with propensity score matching using **MatchThem**. ::: ## What R does by default Most R modelling functions, including `coxph()`, quietly drop every row with a missing value in *any* variable in the model. This is called a **complete-case analysis**. In the `lung` data, a few variables have gaps: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} colSums(is.na(survival::lung)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> inst time status age sex ph.ecog ph.karno pat.karno #> 1 0 0 0 0 1 1 3 #> meal.cal wt.loss #> 47 14 ``` ::: ::: Each gap looks small. But put several of these variables in one model: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ sex + age + ph.ecog + wt.loss + meal.cal, data = survival::lung) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Call: #> coxph(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ sex + age + ph.ecog + wt.loss + #> meal.cal, data = survival::lung) #> #> coef exp(coef) se(coef) z p #> sex -5.400e-01 5.827e-01 1.988e-01 -2.716 0.006602 #> age 8.693e-03 1.009e+00 1.124e-02 0.773 0.439303 #> ph.ecog 5.152e-01 1.674e+00 1.483e-01 3.474 0.000513 #> wt.loss -1.117e-02 9.889e-01 7.548e-03 -1.480 0.138841 #> meal.cal -4.499e-05 1.000e+00 2.512e-04 -0.179 0.857865 #> #> Likelihood ratio test=22.34 on 5 df, p=0.0004517 #> n= 170, number of events= 123 #> (58 observations deleted due to missingness) ``` ::: ::: The last line of the output says it: 58 of the 228 patients (25%) were dropped, and 42 of the 165 deaths. That costs precision, and, as the rest of this chapter shows, it can also bias the results. Always check `n` and `number of events` against the size of your data. ### Practice: how much has the model dropped? *This is a live exercise: edit the code, click **Run Code**, and your answer is checked automatically. See @sec-live-exercises if you haven't used one before.* Add `meal.cal` (calories eaten at meals) to a Cox model for the `lung` data, and find out how many patients the model actually uses. Replace each `______`, then click **Run Code**. ::: {.cell layout-align="center" setup='true' exercise='ex_cc_n'} ```{webr} #| setup: true #| exercise: ex_cc_n library(survival) lung <- survival::lung ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_cc_n' caption='Practice: how much has the model dropped?'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_cc_n #| caption: "Practice: how much has the model dropped?" # Missing values in each column colSums(is.na(lung)) # Cox model with meal.cal added m <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ sex + age + ph.ecog + ______, data = lung) # How many patients did the model use? (last line) m$______ ``` ::: ::: {.hint exercise="ex_cc_n"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint 1 The variable to add is `meal.cal`. ::: ::: ::: {.hint exercise="ex_cc_n"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint 2 The number of patients used is stored in `m$n`. ::: ::: ::: {.solution exercise="ex_cc_n"} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## Solution ```r colSums(is.na(lung)) m <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ sex + age + ph.ecog + meal.cal, data = lung) m$n ``` `meal.cal` is missing for 47 patients, so the model uses only 180 of the 228 patients (and `ph.ecog` drops one more along the way). Nearly a fifth of the data has gone, from a single variable with gaps. ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_cc_n' check='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_cc_n #| check: true m <- .envir_result$m if (!inherits(m, "coxph") || !("meal.cal" %in% all.vars(formula(m)))) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Add meal.cal to the model.") } else if (!is.numeric(.result) || length(.result) != 1 || .result != m$n) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Make the last line m$n, the number of patients used.") } else { list(correct = TRUE, message = sprintf("Correct! The model uses only %d of the 228 patients: %d were dropped because of missing values.", m$n, 228 - m$n)) } ``` ::: ## When does missing data cause bias? It depends on **why** the values are missing. There are three kinds: | Kind | Meaning | Example | Complete-case analysis | |---|---|---|---| | **MCAR**: missing completely at random | Whether a value is missing has nothing to do with the patient | A sample was lost in the post | Unbiased, but wastes data | | **MAR**: missing at random | Whether a value is missing depends on things you **have** recorded | BMI is recorded less often for patients who died, and you know who died | Can be biased. Multiple imputation can fix it | | **MNAR**: missing not at random | Whether a value is missing depends on the missing value itself, or on things you haven't recorded | Heavier patients avoid being weighed | Biased, and no standard method fully fixes it | The names are confusing: "missing at random" doesn't mean the values are missing randomly. It means they're missing at random **once you take account of** the recorded information. For a Cox model, one rule of thumb helps. If whether a covariate is missing depends on the **outcome** (death, or how long patients survived), a complete-case analysis is usually biased. If it depends only on other covariates in the model, a complete-case analysis is usually fine, just less precise. ## A demonstration with a known truth We take the simulated cohort from Chapters 5–7 and delete some BMI values. BMI is recorded less often for patients who **died** (perhaps their final records were incomplete) and for **treated** patients (perhaps they were managed at a different clinic): ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1) p_miss <- plogis(-1.5 + 1.5 * cohort$status + 1 * cohort$treated) cohort_miss <- cohort cohort_miss$bmi[runif(nrow(cohort)) < p_miss] <- NA mean(is.na(cohort_miss$bmi)) # overall ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 0.381 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} tapply(is.na(cohort_miss$bmi), cohort_miss$status, mean) # by death ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> 0 1 #> 0.2735230 0.6152623 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} tapply(is.na(cohort_miss$bmi), cohort_miss$treated, mean) # by treatment ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> 0 1 #> 0.2971329 0.4946996 ``` ::: ::: 38% of BMI values are now missing: 62% among patients who died, and 49% among treated patients. This is **MAR**: the chance of being missing depends on things we have recorded. Compare the covariate-adjusted Cox model fitted to the full data, before anything was deleted, with the complete-case analysis: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} covs <- "treated + age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker" f <- as.formula(paste("Surv(time, status) ~", covs)) full_fit <- coxph(f, data = cohort) # before deleting anything cc_fit <- coxph(f, data = cohort_miss) # complete cases only c(full = exp(coef(full_fit))[["treated"]], complete_case = exp(coef(cc_fit))[["treated"]]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> full complete_case #> 0.6622329 0.5018850 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cc_fit$n ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 1238 ``` ::: ::: With the full data, the treatment HR is 0.66 (the truth, which we built into the data, is 0.70). The complete-case analysis uses only 1238 patients and gives **0.50**, badly exaggerating the benefit. The patients it keeps are not representative: treated patients who died are the most likely to have been dropped. ## Multiple imputation **Multiple imputation** fills in each missing value with a plausible value, predicted from the patient's other information, plus some random variation to reflect our uncertainty. It does this several times, making several complete datasets that differ only in the filled-in values. Then: 1. **Impute:** create $m$ completed datasets (often 10 to 50). 2. **Analyse:** fit the same model to each one. 3. **Pool:** combine the $m$ results with **Rubin's rules**. The pooled estimate is the average of the $m$ estimates. Its standard error combines the uncertainty *within* each analysis with the variation *between* the imputed datasets, so the CI honestly reflects that some values were guessed. The **mice** package does all three. ### Step 1: include the outcome, the right way The imputation model must include **everything in the analysis model, including the outcome**. It feels like cheating to use the outcome to fill in a covariate, but leaving it out biases the results towards no effect. For survival data, don't use the raw follow-up time. Instead, include the event indicator (`status`) and the **Nelson–Aalen estimate** of the cumulative hazard at each patient's follow-up time [@white2009]. `mice` calculates it with `nelsonaalen()`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} cohort_miss$H <- nelsonaalen(cohort_miss, time, status) # The variables used for imputation: the analysis variables, status and H imp_data <- cohort_miss[, c("age", "female", "diabetes", "bmi", "smoker", "treated", "status", "H", "time")] # Keep time in the data (the Cox model needs it), but don't use it to impute pred <- make.predictorMatrix(imp_data) pred[, "time"] <- 0 ``` ::: ### Step 2: impute ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} imp <- mice(imp_data, m = 10, predictorMatrix = pred, seed = 1, printFlag = FALSE) imp$method ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> age female diabetes bmi smoker treated status H #> "" "" "" "pmm" "" "" "" "" #> time #> "" ``` ::: ::: `imp$method` shows how each variable is imputed. Only `bmi` has missing values, and it uses `"pmm"` (*predictive mean matching*): each missing BMI is replaced by an observed BMI from a patient with similar predicted values, so the filled-in values are always realistic. `seed` makes the result reproducible. ### Step 3: analyse and pool ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_mi <- with(imp, coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated + age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker)) pooled <- summary(pool(fit_mi), exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) pooled[, c("term", "estimate", "2.5 %", "97.5 %")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> term estimate 2.5 % 97.5 % #> 1 treated 0.6714700 0.5627439 0.8012029 #> 2 age 1.0669140 1.0576171 1.0762925 #> 3 female 0.8032146 0.6839103 0.9433308 #> 4 diabetes 1.7038476 1.4257359 2.0362094 #> 5 bmi 1.0285074 0.9994750 1.0583832 #> 6 smoker 1.7051351 1.4359722 2.0247506 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip icon="false"} ## How to read this output - `with(imp, coxph(...))` fits the Cox model to each of the 10 completed datasets. - `pool()` combines them with Rubin's rules, and `summary(..., exponentiate = TRUE)` reports hazard ratios. - **estimate** is the pooled HR, and **2.5 %** and **97.5 %** its 95% CI. ::: The pooled HR for treatment is **0.67** (95% CI 0.56 to 0.80), close to the full-data value of 0.66, using all 2000 patients. Multiple imputation has removed the bias that the complete-case analysis introduced. ### Practice: multiple imputation *This is a live exercise: edit the code, click **Run Code**, and your answer is checked automatically. See @sec-live-exercises if you haven't used one before.* The data with missing BMI values are prepared as in this chapter: `imp_data` (including `status` and the Nelson–Aalen estimate `H`) and the predictor matrix `pred`. Impute **5** datasets, fit the Cox model to each, and pool the results. The first run downloads the mice package, which can take a minute. Replace each `______`, then click **Run Code**. ::: {.cell layout-align="center" setup='true' exercise='ex_mi'} ```{webr} #| setup: true #| exercise: ex_mi if (!requireNamespace("mice", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("mice", quiet = TRUE) library(survival) library(mice) simulate_cohort <- function(n = 2000, hr_treat = 0.70, seed = 2026) { set.seed(seed) age <- round(pmin(pmax(rnorm(n, 65, 10), 35), 95)) female <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.45) diabetes <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1.4 + 0.04 * (age - 65))) bmi <- round(rnorm(n, 28, 4.5), 1) smoker <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.25) lp_treat <- -0.6 + 0.06 * (age - 65) + 1.0 * diabetes + 0.08 * (bmi - 28) - 0.3 * female + 0.4 * smoker treated <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lp_treat)) lp_death <- log(hr_treat) * treated + 0.06 * (age - 65) + 0.6 * diabetes + 0.03 * (bmi - 28) - 0.25 * female + 0.55 * smoker shape <- 1.2 lambda <- 0.05 # baseline hazard scale (per year) t_event <- (-log(runif(n)) / (lambda * exp(lp_death)))^(1 / shape) t_admin <- runif(n, 3, 8) # study ends 3-8 years after entry t_dropout <- rexp(n, rate = 0.04) t_cens <- pmin(t_admin, t_dropout) time <- pmin(t_event, t_cens) status <- as.integer(t_event <= t_cens) data.frame( id = seq_len(n), age, female, diabetes, bmi, smoker, treated, time = round(time, 3), status ) } cohort <- simulate_cohort(n = 2000, seed = 2026) set.seed(1) p_miss <- plogis(-1.5 + 1.5 * cohort$status + 1 * cohort$treated) cohort_miss <- cohort cohort_miss$bmi[runif(nrow(cohort)) < p_miss] <- NA cohort_miss$H <- nelsonaalen(cohort_miss, time, status) imp_data <- cohort_miss[, c("age", "female", "diabetes", "bmi", "smoker", "treated", "status", "H", "time")] pred <- make.predictorMatrix(imp_data) pred[, "time"] <- 0 rm(p_miss) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_mi' caption='Practice: multiple imputation'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_mi #| caption: "Practice: multiple imputation" imp <- mice(imp_data, m = ______, predictorMatrix = pred, seed = 1, printFlag = FALSE) fit_mi <- with(imp, coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated + age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker)) summary(______(fit_mi), exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) ``` ::: ::: {.hint exercise="ex_mi"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint 1 `m = 5` creates 5 imputed datasets. ::: ::: ::: {.hint exercise="ex_mi"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint 2 Rubin's rules are applied by `pool()`. ::: ::: ::: {.solution exercise="ex_mi"} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## Solution ```r imp <- mice(imp_data, m = 5, predictorMatrix = pred, seed = 1, printFlag = FALSE) fit_mi <- with(imp, coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated + age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker)) summary(pool(fit_mi), exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) ``` With 5 imputations, the pooled HR for treatment is about 0.68, much closer to the full-data value (0.66) than the complete-case estimate (0.50). With more imputations the result would be a little more stable. ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_mi' check='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_mi #| check: true r <- .result imp <- .envir_result$imp if (!inherits(imp, "mids") || imp$m != 5) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Create 5 imputed datasets: m = 5.") } else if (!inherits(r, "mipo.summary") || !("treated" %in% as.character(r$term)) || r$estimate[as.character(r$term) == "treated"] < 0) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Make the last line summary(pool(fit_mi), exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE).") } else { est <- r$estimate[as.character(r$term) == "treated"] list(correct = TRUE, message = sprintf("Correct! Pooled HR for treatment = %.2f, close to the full-data value of 0.66. The complete-case analysis gave 0.50.", est)) } ``` ::: ## Missing data and propensity score matching Missing confounders cause the same problem for matching: `matchit()` needs complete data, so the complete cases are matched, with the same bias: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # matchit() needs complete data, so keep only the complete cases cc_data <- na.omit(cohort_miss[, c("age", "female", "diabetes", "bmi", "smoker", "treated", "time", "status")]) m_cc <- matchit(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker, data = cc_data, method = "nearest", link = "linear.logit", caliper = 0.2) coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated, data = match.data(m_cc), robust = TRUE, cluster = subclass) |> broom::tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |> select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> # A tibble: 1 x 4 #> term estimate conf.low conf.high #> #> 1 treated 0.562 0.415 0.760 ``` ::: ::: The **MatchThem** package matches *within* each imputed dataset, then pools the results [@pishgar2021]. It works just like `matchit()`, with `datasets = imp` in place of `data`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} mt <- matchthem(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker, datasets = imp, approach = "within", method = "nearest", link = "linear.logit", caliper = 0.2) # Balance, summarised across the 10 imputed datasets bal.tab(mt, binary = "std", thresholds = c(m = 0.1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Balance summary across all imputations #> Type Min.Diff.Adj Mean.Diff.Adj Max.Diff.Adj #> distance Distance 0.0754 0.0843 0.0907 #> age Contin. 0.0325 0.0510 0.0657 #> female Binary -0.0377 0.0014 0.0347 #> diabetes Binary 0.0299 0.0551 0.0857 #> bmi Contin. 0.0096 0.0371 0.0598 #> smoker Binary -0.0339 0.0063 0.0285 #> #> Average sample sizes across imputations #> 0 1 #> All 1151 849 #> Matched 707 707 #> Unmatched 444 142 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_mt <- with(mt, coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated, weights = weights, robust = TRUE, cluster = subclass)) summary(pool(fit_mt), exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)[ , c("term", "estimate", "2.5 %", "97.5 %")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> term estimate 2.5 % 97.5 % #> 1 treated 0.7470145 0.6162722 0.9054938 ``` ::: ::: The complete-case matched HR is 0.56. After multiple imputation and matching within each dataset, it's **0.75** (95% CI 0.62 to 0.91), close to the true marginal HR of about 0.73 from Chapter 7. ## Practical advice - **Look before you analyse.** Count the missing values in each variable, and compare patients with and without missing data, as for loss to follow-up in @sec-informative. - **How many imputations?** A common rule of thumb is at least as many as the percentage of incomplete cases (here 38%, so about 40). Ten is fine for learning. Increase $m$ until the results stop changing. - **What to include.** Every variable in the analysis model, the outcome (`status` and the Nelson–Aalen estimate), and any other variables that predict missingness or the missing values. - **Report it.** Say how much was missing, how you imputed it (method, variables, $m$), and compare with the complete-case analysis. - **MNAR can't be fixed by imputation.** If values are probably missing for reasons you didn't record, say so, and consider a sensitivity analysis that shifts the imputed values up or down. - **When is complete-case analysis fine?** When very little is missing (a few percent), or when missingness depends only on covariates in the model and not on the outcome. ## Quick quiz {.unnumbered} Choose an answer to each question. You'll get instant feedback and can change your answer as often as you like. ```{ojs} //| echo: false import {quiz} from "./js/survtools.js" ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false quiz([ { "q": "A blood test result is missing more often for patients who later died. Death is recorded for everyone. What kind of missingness is this?", "options": ["MCAR", "MAR", "MNAR", "It isn't missing data"], "answer": 1, "why": "Whether the value is missing depends on something that is recorded (death), so it's missing at random given the data. A complete-case Cox analysis is likely to be biased; multiple imputation including the outcome can fix it.", "hints": [ "MCAR would mean missingness has nothing to do with the patient.", "", "MNAR would mean it depends on the missing value itself, or on something not recorded.", "The test result is unknown for these patients." ] }, { "q": "Why should the survival outcome be included when imputing a missing covariate?", "options": [ "Leaving it out biases the covariate's estimated effect towards no effect", "It makes the imputation run faster", "It isn't needed: the outcome should never be used", "Because mice() fails without it" ], "answer": 0, "why": "If the imputation model ignores the outcome, the imputed values have no relationship with it, which dilutes the association. Include status and the Nelson–Aalen estimate.", "hints": [ "", "It's about bias, not speed.", "It feels like cheating, but it's needed to avoid bias.", "mice() runs either way." ] }, { "q": "What does pool() do?", "options": [ "Combines the results from the imputed datasets using Rubin's rules", "Stacks the imputed datasets into one big dataset and fits a single model", "Picks the imputed dataset with the best fit", "Fills in the missing values" ], "answer": 0, "why": "pool() averages the estimates and combines the within- and between-imputation variation into the standard error.", "hints": [ "", "Stacking would make the CI far too narrow.", "Every imputed dataset is used.", "That's what mice() does." ] }, { "q": "A confounder is missing for 30% of patients. You want to use propensity score matching. What is a good approach?", "options": [ "Multiply impute, then match within each imputed dataset and pool (e.g. MatchThem)", "Match the complete cases only", "Replace each missing value with the mean", "Leave the confounder out of the propensity score model" ], "answer": 0, "why": "MatchThem matches within each imputed dataset and pools the effect estimates. Complete cases can be biased, mean imputation understates uncertainty, and leaving out a confounder leaves confounding.", "hints": [ "", "That can be biased, as in this chapter's example (HR 0.56 instead of about 0.73).", "Single mean imputation ignores the uncertainty and can distort relationships.", "Then nothing balances that confounder." ] } ]) ``` ## Summary ::: {.callout-important icon="false"} ## Key points - R drops incomplete rows by default (**complete-case analysis**). Always check `n` and `number of events`. - Missing data are **MCAR**, **MAR** or **MNAR**. If missingness depends on the outcome, complete-case analysis is usually biased. - **Multiple imputation** fills in the gaps several times, analyses each completed dataset, and **pools** the results with Rubin's rules (`mice()`, `with()`, `pool()`). - Include the **outcome** in the imputation model: `status` and the **Nelson–Aalen** cumulative hazard (`nelsonaalen()`), not the raw time. - With propensity score matching, impute first, then match **within** each imputed dataset and pool (**MatchThem**). - Imputation can't fix MNAR. Report how much was missing and what you did, and compare with the complete-case analysis. ::: **Answering the question.** By default, R analyses only the complete cases. When missingness depends on the outcome, that can be badly biased: in our example, the treatment HR was 0.50 instead of 0.66. Multiple imputation, including the outcome correctly, gave 0.67, and the same idea combined with matching gave 0.75 against a true marginal value of about 0.73. ## Further reading All of these are free to read online unless marked otherwise. The whole book's reading list, grouped by topic, is in @sec-further-reading. - @sterne2009: **Start here.** A readable guide to multiple imputation, and how it can go wrong. - @white2009: How to include a survival outcome when imputing covariates for a Cox model (the Nelson–Aalen approach). (May need institutional access.) - @vanbuuren2018: A free online book by the author of mice, from the basics to advanced topics. - @pishgar2021: The MatchThem package, for matching and weighting after multiple imputation.
